action.thought: I have all the evidence I need from the three probes. The canary is clean on errors and on p50/p95, but /search carries a hidden tail: 18/729 (2.47%) requests at 633-656 ms vs a stable /search max of 193 ms, all HTTP 200, spread across all four 30 s windows, while /browse and /checkout are fine. p95 cannot see a 2.5% tail, which is why the dashboard looked green. That is a real, persistent, user-visible regression isolated to the new search path -> ROLLBACK. I avoid the built-in pct() helper (it returned max for every percentile in step 1, i.e. it was being fed row objects) and use an explicit nearest-rank quantile that reproduced the dashboard's numbers in step 3. Expect strings are pinned to deterministic counts and booleans rather than fragile float formatting.

The decision file is already written with ROLLBACK plus claims whose queries I executed in steps 2-3, and their outputs printed the expect strings. Nothing left to verify in the data, so the correct next action is to finish and let the harness validate the file.

args.summary: Decision: ROLLBACK, written to review/D-evidence-2/decision.json. Evidence from run_query over this canary's request log: (1) 18 of 729 canary /search requests took 633-656 ms while 0 of 2273 stable /search requests exceeded 200 ms (stable /search max 193 ms); canary /search p99 = 652 ms vs stable 61 ms (ratio >= 8x) while p50 is identical at 47 ms - a pure tail regression that the dashboard's aggregate p95 (95 vs 95) hides. (2) The slow requests span all four 30 s windows (counts 7,2,5,4; first t=3.2 s, last t=113.3 s), so it is sustained, not a warm-up artifact. (3) No error signal: all slow responses are status 200, canary 5xx = 0, stable 5xx = 0. (4) Other paths are not worse on the canary: /browse p99 30 ms vs 28 ms, /checkout p99 105 ms vs 106 ms. Judgement: ~2.5% of /search served at ~0.65 s, reproducible across the whole test and absent on stable, is a real user-visible regression, so block the release rather than send 100% of traffic to 1.1; follow up by profiling the new version's /search tail before re-running the canary.
